processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Steel blocks were cast via vacuum arc furnace.
Promotes uniform composition and microstructure throughout the steel blocks.
Homogenized steel subjected to step-by-step hot rolling reducing thickness to ~11 mm, followed by slow cooling in the oven.

processing_steps.method: water jet cutting (OMAX 2626, Kent, Washington, USA)
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Samples precisely fabricated by water jet cutting to allow accurate geometries and minimize thermal distortion. Cylindrical specimens (ø5 x 10 mm³) were used for heat treatments in the DIL 805A dilatometer.

S3 required the higher schedule of 1220 °C to minimize αp and to approach the simulated ferrite-free field; a fully αp-free condition could not be realized. Fig. 1(a) prints 'S3 : 1220 °C (20 min.)'. Heating rate 10 K s⁻¹.

processing_steps.method: cooling from austenitization to austempering temperature
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: The cooling rate from austenitization to the austempering temperature was 100 K s⁻¹, sufficiently fast to suppress intermediate phase transformations.

Austempered at TB = 270 °C (just above the measured Ms = 258 °C) with an incubation time of 120 s and a slow bainite growth period of nearly 3000 s following incubation; transformation extended to approximately 43,000 s (Bt = 43000 s in Fig. 6(d)). LOM at 270 °C for 25,200 s remained incomplete; 43,200 s was required for near-complete transformation.
Final cooling step of the thermal cycle shown in Fig. 1(a), after the isothermal bainitic hold.

structures.overall_structure: Multiphase microstructure of nano-bainitic steel S3 after austenitizing at 1220 °C and austempering at 270 °C: a bainitic ferrite (αb) matrix with retained austenite (γr) at lath boundaries (partly blocky/sluggish γr in transformation-free micro-regions) plus an unavoidable residual polygonal ferrite (αp) fraction of 8.2 %, together with (Fe,M)xCy precipitates located near γr–bainitic ferrite boundaries and nanoscale non-stoichiometric L12-type κ-carbide embedded in the matrix.
structures.number_of_phases: ≥4 (bainitic ferrite, retained austenite, polygonal ferrite, (Fe,M)xCy carbides; plus nanoscale κ-carbide and AlN)

phases_present.morphology: nano-bainitic laths; true lamellar thickness Lt(t) = 40 nm (SD 10 nm); lenticular sheaves with impingement of bainite sheaves; higher SD at higher TB indicates nB Type 1 and Type 2 alongside blocky γr

blocky γr regions between bainitic sheaves; partially decomposed sluggish γr in some micro-regions; in S3 at 270 °C the higher average εγ (0.54 %) versus ferritic phases (0.33 %) indicates pronounced strain partitioning and dislocation accumulation in the metastable γr

ferrite plates predominantly allotriomorphic, occasionally idiomorphic; α or δ nature remains unclear; could not be eliminated even at 1220 °C; area fraction was ~14.6 % at 1050 °C and ~8.2 % at 1220 °C

defects.lattice_distortion: εγ 0.54 %, εα 0.33 % (phase-resolved microstrain; pronounced heterogeneity of dislocation distribution at 270 °C)

precipitates.type: (Fe,M)xCy (cementite-like carbide with M = Si, Mo; Al essentially absent)
precipitates.distribution: located near the γr–bainitic ferrite phase boundaries; only detectable due to localized brightness under SEM; TTP calculation shows a slight increase in (Fe,M)xCy in S3 compared to S1 and S2

structures.overall_structure: Prior-austenitization reference state: at the 1050 °C benchmark temperature S3 exhibited extensive polygonal ferrite (αp) in a dark-etched matrix (area fraction ~14.6 %), which persisted at 1220 °C (~8.2 %), consistent with the very high Al content and the simulated requirement of ~1177 °C to approach a ferrite-free state.

phases_present.morphology: abundant light polygonal ferrite islands in a dark matrix (LOM); occasionally idiomorphic but predominantly allotriomorphic ferrite plates

defect_interactions.interaction_type: strain partitioning / dislocation accumulation in retained austenite
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: At 270 °C the phase-resolved microstrain differed markedly between γr and bainitic ferrite (εγ: 0.54 % vs. εα: 0.33 %), consistent with pronounced strain partitioning; the significantly higher ε in the metastable γr indicates pronounced dislocation accumulation, leading to the formation of highly brittle phase boundaries and potential stress-spiking regions, which explains the severe drop in elongation to 2.4 %.

defect_interactions.interaction_type: carbon partitioning / bainite growth stalling at αp–austenite interfaces
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: αp can serve as nucleation sites for bainitic transformation, but its low C solubility leads to significant C-partitioning into the adjacent austenite (C-enrichment), locally stabilizing the austenite and increasing the energy barrier around αp plates. Initial nucleation was observed at αp–austenite interfaces, but bainite growth could not propagate and stalled at many sites, leaving transformation-free regions that required much longer holding times (25,200 s incomplete; 43,200 s near-complete).

interfaces.phase_evolution: During austempering at 270 °C of S3: bainite nucleates at αp–austenite interfaces but growth stalls; C-enrichment around αp stabilizes adjacent austenite, producing partially decomposed sluggish γr and transformation-free regions; only a prolonged duration (~43,000 s) achieves near-complete bainitic transformation.
interfaces.interface_notes: (Fe,M)xCy precipitates are located near the γr–bainitic ferrite phase boundaries; highly brittle phase boundaries and stress-spiking regions form because of the imbalanced dislocation distribution; Si entrapped in the Fe-based carbide lattice and Mo enhance precipitate stability, inhibiting void formation.

measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: ASTM E8 sub-size round tensile specimens (12.5 mm gauge length, 2.5 mm diameter, 7 mm shoulder length)
measurement_conditions.other_conditions: All tensile specimens were heat-treated using the DIL 805A dilatometer applying the thermal cycle of Fig. 1(a), with austenitizing at 1220 °C and austempering at TB = 270 °C just above the measured Ms of 258 °C.

comparative_performance.comparison_metric: bainitic transformation finish time (Bt): S3 (highest Al ~8 wt.%) is the slowest of all steels (Bt: 14,000–43,000 s depending on austempering temperature) whereas S5 is the fastest (Bt: 700–1000 s); S1/S2 are intermediate (Bt: 1600–4000 s) and S4 is 3000–3500 s

El at TB 350 °C vs TB 270 °C for S3: El 8.2 % at 350 °C (UTS 1360 MPa) versus El 2.4 % at 270 °C (UTS 1450 MPa); PSE drops from ~11,150 MPa·% to ~3480 MPa·%; the 8.08 wt.% Al design is detrimental to ductility at lower TB

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Carl Zeiss AG, Jena, Germany; samples etched with 6 % Nital solution; ImageJ (v1.53, NIH, Bethesda, MD, USA) used for quantitative image analysis of primary αp volume fraction and spatial distribution (200× micrographs from five distinct regions) — performed only for steel S3
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: etched samples, 200× magnification, five distinct regions; LOM at 1050 °C benchmark and at the selected TA = 1220 °C
characterization_methods.purpose: reveal microstructural features (particularly due to the high Al content) and quantify the primary αp volume fraction and spatial distribution of S3
characterization_methods.key_findings: S3 shows extensive polygonal ferrite: area fraction ~14.6 % at 1050 °C and ~8.2 % at 1220 °C; residual αp marked by labelled arrows at 1220 °C; at 270 °C the transformation remained incomplete at Bt = 25,200 s and was near-complete at 43,200 s; αp plates are occasionally idiomorphic but predominantly allotriomorphic (Fig. 9(h),(i))

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Carl Zeiss AG, Jena, Germany; gold sputter coating applied to etched samples; ImageJ used to determine bainite thickness (100 measurements from 10 SEM images per specimen, 10 per image); true lamellar thickness Lt(t) = 2Lt/π (stereological correction)
characterization_methods.purpose: characterize bainitic morphology, measure bainite lamellar thickness, and detect precipitates
characterization_methods.key_findings: For S3 austempered at 350 °C (5 µm images) and 270 °C (5 µm images): mixed lath and blocky structure with impingement of bainite sheaves, αp, lenticular sheaves with dark blocky regions, sluggish γr (label 6) and (Fe,M)xCy precipitate at a grain-boundary junction; rounded (Fe,M)xCy precipitates with no micro-void formation

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Oxford Instruments, Abingdon, UK, attached to the Carl Zeiss SEM; quantitative carbon content not measurable (C only used to detect (Fe,M)xCy)
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: S3 austempered at 270 °C (Fig. 9(g) SEM for EDX analysis targeting Spec.4, Spec.5, Spec.6); also used for the precipitates shown in Fig. 9(b),(c),(g)
characterization_methods.purpose: determine the composition of precipitates and confirm their identity in S3
characterization_methods.key_findings: EDX identifies Spec.4 as AlN in S3 at 270 °C; the rounded (Fe,M)xCy particles show essentially no Al, with M = Si, Mo; Si entrapped within the Fe-based carbide lattice due to rapid cooling; C detected only qualitatively

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Malvern Panalytical Empyrean diffractometer with Cu X-ray tube, operated at 40 kV/40 mA with a PIXcel 1D detector (TU Clausthal Institute of Non-Metallic Materials); mechanically grinded and polished samples; ASTM E975-13 guidelines
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Cu Kα radiation, 40 kV/40 mA; retained austenite volume fraction and microstrains (εγ for austenite, εα for bainitic ferrite) determined from (111)γ, (200)γ, (220)γ and (311)γ peak integrated intensities; Vγ = (1 - Vc)(Iγ/Rγ)/[(Iα/Rα)+(Iγ/Rγ)]
characterization_methods.purpose: determine the volume fraction of retained austenite (Vγ) and the phase microstrains (εγ, εα)
characterization_methods.key_findings: For S3 at TA 1220 °C / TB 270 °C: Vγ = 29 %, εγ = 0.54 %, εα = 0.33 %, indicating pronounced strain partitioning and heterogeneous dislocation distribution

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: Carl Zeiss SEM (Carl Zeiss AG, Jena, Germany) equipped with an Oxford Instruments EBSD system and software; specimens ground, electropolished and vibratory polished to obtain a deformation-free surface
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: accelerating voltage 20 kV, step size 0.2 µm (selected according to microstructural feature size)
characterization_methods.purpose: evaluate microstructure/phase constitution and grain/interface characteristics
characterization_methods.key_findings: EBSD is under-counting γr relative to XRD in fine lath structures because the film-like γr at bainite lath boundaries is near or below the EBSD step size; XRD is therefore taken as quantitative for phase fractions (reported mainly for S5 and the general characterization of the steels)

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: DIL 805A dilatometer (TA Instruments, New Castle, DE, USA); cylindrical specimens (ø5 x 10 mm³)
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: heating at 10 K s⁻¹ (with 1 K s⁻¹ above 1100 °C for TA detection), cooling at 100 K s⁻¹; isothermal austempering holds
characterization_methods.purpose: determine the austenitizing temperature (TA), the martensite start temperature (Ms) by tangent-intersection analysis of the RLC curves, and the bainitic transformation finish time (Bt) from the onset of the RLC plateau
characterization_methods.key_findings: For S3: broadened austenitizing transition without a unique TA (no single sharp break; operational line near 880 °C in the derivative plot); Ms = 258 °C after austenitizing at 1220 °C (lowest Ms of the studied steels); Bt ≈ 43,000 s at TB = 270 °C (and ≈ 14,000 s at 350 °C)

computational_details.simulation_method: thermodynamic equilibrium (step) calculation and precipitation-kinetics simulation (Time-Temperature-Precipitation, TTP, diagrams)
computational_details.software_used: MatCalc (Version: 6.01 (rel 1.003), Institute of Materials Science and Technology, TU Wien, Wien, Austria)
computational_details.potential_model_or_database: equilibrium/kinetic description of the phase synergy of fcc, bcc, liquid, κ-carbide, hcp carbide, AlN and TiCN–TiMoC systems; Ti–Mo–C and (Fe,M)xCy carbide systems simulated with a precipitation kinetics model based on heterogeneous nucleation theory (dislocation and grain-boundary sites only, ortho-equilibrium transformation), accounting for volumetric misfit; κ-carbides treated as fixed phase fractions (spinodal decomposition) and thus excluded from classical nucleation theory
computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: cooling rate 100 K s⁻¹; heat treatment defining the bainitic transformation for S3 (TA: 1220 °C, TB: 350 °C and TB: 270 °C, Bt: 14,000 s and 43,000 s)
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Simulated ferrite-free TA (1177 °C) and carbide-dissolution temperature (Tcd ≈ 1103 °C) for S3 were used together with dilatometry and LOM to select the applied TA of 1220 °C; TTP prediction of (Fe,M)xCy formation above the austempering temperature agrees with the SEM/EDX precipitate observations; the slight increase in (Fe,M)xCy in S3 versus S1/S2 (attributed to the higher Al content) is assessed as having negligible impact on mechanical properties

analytical_models.model_name: Eq. 1 — retained austenite volume fraction from integrated XRD intensities
analytical_models.equation_role: Vγ = (1 - Vc)(Iγ/Rγ)/[(Iα/Rα)+(Iγ/Rγ)], used to compute the retained-austenite volume fraction while accounting for the carbide fraction Vc
analytical_models.model_note: Applied to the S3 XRD data; the carbide fraction Vc was taken from MatCalc equilibrium phase diagrams, with (1 - Vc) as the total (bainitic ferrite + γr) fraction

unmapped_findings: Chemical composition of steel S3 (wt.%): C 1.05, Al 8.08, Mn 1.00, Si 0.30, Mo 0.50, B 0.0039; Ni and Ti not added (Table 1; Al content highest of the studied steels).
S3 austenitizing temperatures: MatCalc ferrite-free TA = 1177 °C; measured TA = broadened transition without a unique value; applied TA = 1220 °C (Table 2 / Fig. 2).

S3 martensite start temperature Ms = 258 °C measured by cooling dilatometry after austenitizing at 1220 °C — the lowest Ms among the studied steels, consistent with extended κ-carbide dissolution and ferrite retention facilitating local carbon partitioning into austenite.

S3 carbide-dissolution temperature Tcd ≈ 1103 °C from MatCalc equilibrium phase-fraction simulation; the simulated ferrite-free TA of ~1177 °C could not be fully achieved in practice (residual αp 8.2 % at 1220 °C).

S3 product of strength and elongation (PSE) ≈ 3480 MPa·% (≈ 3.5 GPa·%) at TB 270 °C (UTS 1450 MPa, El 2.4 %) and ~11,150 MPa·% at TB 350 °C (UTS 1360 MPa, El 8.2 %) — the lowest PSE of the study at 270 °C.

S3 transformation kinetics: Bt ≈ 43,000 s at TB 270 °C (incubation 120 s, slow bainite growth period ~3000 s) and Bt ≈ 14,000 s at TB 350 °C (incubation 140 s, slow growth period ~1500 s); the slow transformation is attributed to C-enrichment and stabilization of austenite around polygonal ferrite.

Bainitic transformation times of the comparison steels for context: S5 (fastest, Bt 700–1000 s), S1/S2 (Bt 1600–4000 s), S4 Ti-microalloyed (Bt 3000–3500 s); S3 with ~8 wt.% Al is the slowest (Bt 14,000–43,000 s); small Ni addition (0.78 wt.% in S4 and S5) did not affect transformation time.

Hardness values reported in Fig. 7 for the eleven TA/TB conditions (left to right: 464, 497, 465, 500, 443, 457, 464, 479, 467, 459, 493 HV30); the S3, TA: 1220 °C, TB: 270 °C condition corresponds to 457 HV30, consistent with the statement that hardness (450–500 HV30) is higher at lower TB except for S4.

SEM/EDX of S3 identified, besides (Fe,M)xCy, an AlN particle (Spec.4) in the 270 °C condition, and Al contents within particles were essentially absent, indicating a nucleation-driven (not spinodal) formation mechanism.

κ-carbide (E21-type stoichiometric perovskite) was not directly examined microscopically in S3; its absence of observable structures is attributed to the limited Mn content (≈1 wt.%), with remaining κ-carbides presumed to exist as nanoscale, embedded, non-stoichiometric L12-type structures.
